entries.title: Democrats in Congress Don't Like Shri Thanedar. He Hopes Voters Disagree.
entries.summary: The lawmaker faces a democratic socialist challenger in a blue Detroit-area district.
entries.content:
How much does it matter if a lawmaker’s colleagues are indifferent about him in Congress?

According to Rep. Shri Thanedar, a wealthy lawmaker who represents Michigan’s 13th Congressional District and who has become one of the left’s targets, not much. The popularity contest that matters is among voters rather than his congressional peers. 

On Tuesday, voters will choose between Thanedar and Donavan McKinney, a young, Black state lawmaker and democratic socialist who grew up poor in Detroit.

The House primary has flashes of the different identity crises Democrats are facing this year: How left is too left? Is being an incumbent a net negative when voters are this angry? How important is racial representation?

Then there's the one unique twist: Not even Thanedar's colleagues know what to make of him, which he concedes.

“It's not like a high school,” Thanedar, acknowledging apathy from his colleagues about his primary challenge, told NOTUS. “I’m not trying to be the most popular member of Congress.”

Thanedar, who emigrated from India in 1979 and worked as a janitor until he became a pharmaceutical executive, is arguing that he should keep his job in Congress because he understands the struggles his district faces. While some of his colleagues have said that they do not care whether he leaves Congress, he has the backing of party leaders, including Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar.

“My constituents know my story,” Thanedar said. “They know my struggles, and I am more like Detroit because Detroit has struggled, but Detroit never gives up.”

McKinney, meanwhile, is campaigning on “Medicare for All,” a Green New Deal and ending American military aid to Israel. He’s backed by Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont), numerous state lawmakers, local government officials and progressive groups like Sunrise Movement and Justice Democrats.

His campaign is hoping to carry the momentum created by progressive victories across the country, including in several New York City House primaries and Colorado’s 1st Congressional District, to a battleground state.

“People think this movement is just in New York or just in California or just in certain states,” McKinney said. “This is across the board, and you can win purple states like Michigan. You can win in Middle America. You can win in toss-up country.”

One example of how much he’s leaning into the anti-incumbency sentiment is his reluctance to support Jeffries as speaker of the House if Democrats win the chamber.

“I don’t have a decision yet. I just want a conversation,” he said. He added that while he’d love to see a Black speaker, he wonders if Jeffries can help Democrats keep the majority next cycle. “How long does he want to be speaker if he actually gets elected speaker?”

Other primary races in Michigan are also testing how progressives perform in a purple state. Climate activist Will Lawrence is hoping to defeat two centrist Democrats in a swing district — but if he pulls it off, Democrats are wary of his chances of beating Republican Rep. Tom Barrett. The state’s marquee Senate primary also has establishment Democrats sweating over whether their pick, Rep. Haley Stevens, will beat out progressive Abdul El-Sayed.

But this primary is where groups like Justice Democrats, who tapped McKinney as its first recruit of the cycle, are hoping to close the loop.

“[This primary] embodies the entire fight that we are having in the broader Democratic Party right now, which is — are we going to be a party that is represented by multimillionaires serving the interests of billionaires, or are we going to let working class communities be represented by working class people?” said Usamah Andrabi, the group’s spokesperson.

Many Democrats in the district think Thanedar secured his last two wins because the Black vote was split among multiple candidates, making this head-to-head matchup a serious threat to the incumbent.

The race isn’t a clean split between progressives and establishment Democrats. The district has a long history of Black representation, and that has prompted several members of the Congressional Black Caucus, like Reps. Summer Lee (D-Pennsylvania) and Steven Horsford (D-Nevada), to break with Jeffries and other party leaders in endorsing McKinney over their colleague.

Several Black state lawmakers in Michigan are also rallying behind McKinney. The Supreme Court’s dismantling key protections of the Voting Rights Act and the elimination of majority-minority districts around the country through redistricting are motivating voters to support him, McKinney said.

“Allies are allies, but unless you’ve lived what I've lived, you won't be able to advocate the way I'm able to advocate,” said state Rep. Stephanie Young, chair of the Detroit Caucus in the statehouse and a McKinney supporter.

Thanedar said that Black constituents supporting him in the race are doing so because of his track record.

“For them, it’s not about the race of the candidate. It's about who can help them, who can bring more federal dollars home,” he said. “Their concern is about who can fight hardest against Trump, and there's nobody fighting harder than me against Trump and the Trump administration.”

He also has six members of the CBC backing him, including Reps. Bennie Thompson (D-Mississippi) and Cleo Fields (D-Louisiana).

Asked if he wished he had more support from members of Congress, Thanedar said, “No, no, I have plenty.”

There’s also the matter of financing.

While Thanedar largely self-financed his campaign, he has been criticized by his opponent for being financially supported by the American Israel Public Affairs Committee and crypto industry. Thanedar rejected the idea that he is indebted to corporate donors and pointed to progressive super PACs like American Priorities, a pro-Palestine super PAC meant to counter AIPAC, spending on McKinney’s behalf.

Thanedar’s campaign had about $5 million in the bank on July 15, according to a pre-primary Federal Election Commission report, and he loaned his campaign $2.1 million. McKinney has raised $1.3 million and had nearly $143,000 in the bank as of July 15.

For McKinney, funding is a key part of his pitch of why he should replace Thanedar in Congress.

“This election is about the many versus the money,” he said.
entries.author: Christa Dutton

entries.title: Montgomery County Approved New School Boundaries. Parents Won’t Let It End There.
entries.summary: Some residents are pursuing a legal challenge to the planned closure of the highly rated Wootton High School.
entries.content:
A smattering of “Save Wootton” and “It’s Not Over!” yard signs dot neighborhoods surrounding the Rockville, Maryland, high school whose name and student body are due to be transferred in 2027-28 to a new building several miles away.

With the Montgomery County Board of Education having approved the shift last spring, the red, white and blue signs — matching the colors of Thomas S. Wootton High School — remain as a defiant statement by residents, some of whom are pursuing a legal challenge to plans they say would illegally close the highly rated, half-century-old school in the Washington suburbs.

“It’s such a necessity,” said Rockville Council member Adam Van Grack, whose son attends Wootton. “It’s not a question of if it’s going to be a permanent school again, the only question is when.”

A dozen miles away, similar yard signs remain in the neighborhood around the sprawling Silver Spring International Middle School, which area residents fear isn’t in the county’s future plans.

“The school gives us an opportunity to greet one another. It gives us a sense of community," said Angie Kronenberg, an attorney who, during the campaign's busiest periods, devoted as many as 30 to 40 hours a week organizing efforts to preserve the school, which is adjacent to Silver Spring’s downtown and home to sought-after Spanish and French immersion programs.

Montgomery County, home to Maryland’s largest public school system, completed sweeping boundary studies in March that upended the futures of Wootton and Silver Spring International, and redrew boundaries for other schools to account for enrollment shifts, school building conditions and other factors.

But the school assignment debates never quite seem over, and in the case of Wootton, parents and community members have lodged complaints over everything from deteriorating building conditions to property values.

Boundary shifts stir powerful protective instincts, said Sarah Asson, a senior researcher at the nonprofit research group Education Northwest, often turning parents into activists fighting for what they view as their children's best interests.

“These rezonings touch two of the most important things for parents -– their kids’ education and their communities,” Asson said.

While parents typically frame their objections around their children's education and their communities, issues regarding image and status are often at play as well, said Genevieve Siegel-Hawley, a professor in Virginia Commonwealth University’s School of Education.

“There is a lot of anxiety — status anxiety — about securing their kids’ futures through education,” Siegel-Hawley said.
DC0A5520 copy.jpg (7772x5182, AR: 1.50)Real estate values can also be an important, if less openly acknowledged, subtext. Homes assigned to highly regarded schools often command a premium, and some residents worry boundary changes will diminish their property values.

Wootton, which has about 1,900 students, is one of the county’s prestigious, so-called “W” schools along with high-achieving Walt Whitman, Walter Johnson and Winston Churchill. It is not uncommon for families in the more diverse eastern portion of the county, including Silver Spring and Wheaton, to move to the western part so their kids can attend a “W” or the highly rated Bethesda-Chevy Chase High School.

“For 20-some years if I had a property in the Wootton school district, I hardly had to say anything about the house. I just said ‘Wootton,’ and it had this magnetic attraction for buyers,” said Kevin Grolig, a real estate agent in the county.

If plans to move Wootton remain intact, Grolig estimates that values of homes within walking distance of the school’s current location could drop 15% or more.

Wootton remains open for now. An oversized “Wootton Strong” banner hangs from the back of the football field bleachers.

But the school, whose former students include actor Thomas Jane, NFL player Trevon Diggs and several members of the rock band O.A.R., was built in 1970 and has issues with leaking ceilings, heating and cooling units and mice.

On March 26, the county Board of Education voted 7-1 to approve moving Wootton to a new school in Gaithersburg for the 2027-28 school year. Thomas Taylor, the superintendent of Montgomery County Public schools, said a single school could efficiently handle current enrollment and that the old Wootton would be employed as a “holding school” for when other schools are undergoing construction.

At the meeting, parents held signs reading “Don’t Close Wootton” and “Vote No,” and some parents chanted “shame” when the vote was complete.

“This is not a closure of Thomas S. Wootton High School — this is a move of the school to a new building,” said a Montgomery County Public Schools announcement in February explaining the plan.

It said Wootton students “will transition to a state-of-the-art facility” and that the system was responding “to updated enrollment data showing needs can be met more efficiently with the current number of schools.”

But critics said importing the school’s name, colors and “Patriots” mascot to a new building won’t make it the real Wootton, but rather a weird facsimile.
DC0A5489 copy.jpg (8192x5464, AR: 1.50)
In April, a nonprofit group composed of Wootton parents, alumni and others filed an administrative appeal with the Maryland State Board of Education challenging the March decision.

“At the heart of the appeal is a straightforward question: Can a school board avoid Maryland’s statutory school closure requirements by characterizing a school closure as a ‘relocation?’” the group said in a prepared statement.

The case is pending. Montgomery County Public Schools said it could not comment on any litigation.

The school system declined to make Taylor available for an interview or answer NOTUS’ questions about possible scenarios for the futures of Wootton and Silver Spring International.

Rather, Montgomery County Public Schools emailed a statement about the new two-year, elementary and middle school boundary study. The statement said the study will address “system-wide facility capacity, optimize building utilization and evaluate potential school closures or consolidations" with community input.

Last year, the county Board of Education declined to pursue Taylor’s recommendation to convert Silver Spring International, whose buildings are in deteriorating condition, into a holding school. While the school wasn’t targeted for closure in the March vote, many parents say the board’s decision to reduce its number of feeder elementary schools has placed the school on an uncertain path because its enrollment will decline.

Proponents of maintaining Silver Spring International and Wootton often raise concerns that are difficult to quantify. Some speak nostalgically of the quiet ritual of children being close enough to walk to their neighborhood schools.

“That was the number one thing parents were saying to me: ‘Our kids can still walk to school, right?’” said Kronenberg, who helps lead a Silver Spring group called “Save Our Schools.”

“We believe our school is still at risk,” Kronenberg said. "We have to keep at it."
entries.author: Jeff Barker

entries.title: What $800K Gets You in D.C., Maryland and Virginia
entries.summary: Our weekly column compares home listings across the metro area.
entries.content:
A penthouse condo in Columbia Heights. A spacious townhouse in North Bethesda. A cozy and convenient house in Arlington. Here’s what $800,000 gets you in the District, Maryland and Virginia.

(Which one would you choose? Or, have a comparison you’d like to see in an upcoming column? Let us know at metro@notus.com.)

D.C.

Untitled
The Listing: 1223 Kenyon St. NW #3

The Price: $799,900

The Specifics: This two-bedroom, two-bathroom penthouse condo comes in at just over 1,300 square feet, and features a private rooftop deck in addition to parking spaces for two cars. The home also includes a spacious primary bedroom with a spa-like bath, walk-in shower and dual vanities, according to the listing. The real estate agent also highlights the home’s solid oak hardwood floors, modern finishes and open-concept living.

The Neighborhood: This home is in the heart of Columbia Heights, within a short walk to the neighborhood’s Metro station with access to the Green and Yellow lines. Also nearby are a number of fitness studios and grocery stores, in addition to popular bars and restaurants like Wonderland Ballroom and St. Vincent Wine. The neighborhood itself is densely populated and known for its historic row houses and cultural diversity.

Maryland

Untitled
The Listing: 10719 Gloxinia Drive, Rockville

The Price: $775,000

The Specifics: This spacious townhome comes in around 2,500 square feet, with the real estate agent describing it as “a rare blend of timeless character, effortless open-concept living, and modern peace of mind.” The three-bedroom, five-bathroom home has only had two previous owners, and features a secluded private courtyard. Recent updates in the home include a new roof, new HVAC and new doors, according to the listing.

The Neighborhood: The home is in North Bethesda, and is 10-minute drive from the Bethesda Trolley Trail and just five minutes from Pike & Rose, a shopping and entertainment area featuring restaurants, a movie theater and live music venues. It’s also a short drive from the North Bethesda Metro station, with access to D.C. via the Red Line.

Virginia

Untitled
The Listing: 3917 6th St. S., Arlington

The Price: $799,000

The Specifics: This home offers just over 1,000 square feet of room with three bedrooms and two full bathrooms. The lower level features hardwood floors, while the upper level is carpeted. The basement is unfinished, making it the perfect spot for storage or a workshop. The shaded and spacious backyard features raised gardening beds and a storage shed.

The Neighborhood: This Arlington home is located in the Alcova Heights neighborhood, which is known for its proximity to Columbia Pike, connecting Northern Virginia to D.C for a commute the real estate agent describes as “effortless.” The home is also conveniently close to Alcova Heights Park, shopping centers and restaurants.

entries.title: How Politicians Living and Dead Play the Stock Market With Campaign Cash
entries.summary: Opaque investments boost lawmakers’ campaign coffers with little public oversight.
entries.content:
Former Speaker of the House Tom Foley lost his final bid for reelection in 1994 after three decades in office.

In 2013, Foley died.

But the “Committee to Reelect Tom Foley” — his still-technically active campaign committee — lives on, and it reported earning a small profit this year from several financial investments, including stock in tech giants Microsoft and Meta.

Foley’s old committee stands among scores of federal campaign operations that reap the rewards of invested campaign funds, a NOTUS review of federal records indicates.

For prolific fundraisers, including current members of Congress, such investments can yield six- or seven-figure windfalls annually, with political figures of all partisan leanings making sometimes lucrative stock and financial gambles using money donors gave their campaigns for election purposes.

There are no set limits on the amount of money campaigns can earn by investing donor cash, giving politicians an added — although potentially risky — tool for boosting their campaign coffers beyond traditional fundraising methods.

Campaign committees’ investments are often secretive, too: Few campaigns report details beyond a dollar figure and their bank or investment house of choice. This leaves voters unable to determine whether a political campaign’s specific investments could potentially conflict with a candidate’s official duties, such as a member of Congress who oversees military matters while investing campaign cash in defense contractor stocks.

While members of Congress are notorious for making improperly disclosed personal stock trades while in office, their penchant for using campaign cash to play the markets is far less scrutinized and, often, even more opaque.

NOTUS attempted to contact the campaigns of nearly 150 current members of Congress to ask whether they would voluntarily share details about their campaign committees’ specific financial investments.

Only five responded, and those who did said their investments were conservative — largely just earning interest from bank accounts.

Investors of the 119th Congress

It makes sense for candidates with hundreds of thousands, if not millions, of dollars in their campaign accounts to park their cash somewhere where it can accumulate interest over time, if only to defend against inflation.

Many federal candidates report steady earnings consistent with conservative investment accounts such as money market funds or certificates of deposit.

Rep. Chuck Fleischmann (R-Tennessee), for example, has reported stable monthly yields between $10,000 and $13,000 in “bank interest” for the past two years. For over two decades, both Senate Majority Leader John Thune and Minority Leader Chuck Schumer have earned steady interest from the millions of surplus dollars sitting in their campaign accounts.

The campaign of Rep. Julia Brownley (D-California) stores its money in a “non-traditional bond fund,” two high-yield bond funds and “short term CDs,” a campaign spokesperson said.

For candidates who invest their campaign money more aggressively, many have good months … and bad months.

In February, the campaign of Rep. Bill Foster (D-Illinois) reported a $16,525 “investment gain.” But in March, he reported a $21,356 “investment loss.”

Other lawmakers’ campaign portfolios swing wildly from quarter to quarter.

In November 2024, the campaign of Rep. Shri Thanedar (D-Michigan) reported $1.9 million in “investment income.” In February 2025, it reported a $1.2 million “loss.” Mounting losses across this election cycle caused his cash on hand to fall more than $1.8 million — a remarkable drop for a campaign already $13.6 million in debt to Thanedar himself. Last quarter, his campaign reported a loss of $634,129, which it labeled "Investment Income Loss from a mutual fund."
Election 2022 House Detroit AP-22215573683258 (3000x2133, AR: 1.41)Representatives for Thanedar, who faces a competitive Democratic primary in August, did not respond to a request for comment.

In 2025, Thanedar vowed to personally stop trading individual stocks after NOTUS reported that he violated the federal Stop Trading on Congressional Knowledge Act’s disclosure provision with improperly disclosed personal trades.

“Members of Congress should not trade in individual stocks,” Thanedar told NOTUS at the time. “Many of my individual stock purchases I did are from years before I was in Congress. My goal is to get rid of all the individual stocks in my portfolio, but it takes time.”

In a single December 2024 filing, Sen. Lindsey Graham, who died in July, reported more than $1.1 million from "investment account earnings" and another $229,000 in dividends. Graham’s campaign committee had $2.3 million in remaining cash, with several options for disposing of it.
Lindsey Graham AP - 26045665775855 (8256x5504, AR: 1.50)Sen. Dick Durbin (D-Illinois) faced criticism during the 2008 financial crisis for dumping much of his personal stock holdings as markets reeled and Congress prepared relief legislation. Federal filings show his personal campaign, in contrast, was months ahead of the curve, selling its stocks in May 2008 and netting $137,471 in the process.

Nowadays, Durbin’s campaign nets about $100 a month in basic interest.

What’s legal, what’s not

The reporting requirements for trading using campaign cash are far less stringent than what lawmakers are obligated to disclose when making financial trades that affect their own personal finances.

It's generally easy to spot possible conflicts of interest when lawmakers who have jurisdiction over specific industries buy and sell shares of companies directly affected by their actions. That’s because the STOCK Act requires them to publicly detail and disclose within 45 days any stock, bond or cryptocurrency trade that they make in their personal capacity.

That same scrutiny cannot be applied to those lawmakers when they trade using their campaign funds under the current rules.

“The current opaque investment income for campaigns conceal potential conflicts of interests from the media and voters, such as campaign investing in the personal business interests of the candidate or candidate’s family,” Public Citizen lobbyist Craig Holman said. “If campaigns are enriching their own pockets or those of political friends, that is information that donors and voters would want to know.”

“The requirements also need to be enhanced to provide the full picture of investment income by campaigns, much in the same way as personal financial disclosure requirements placed on officeholders,” Holman said.

Some lawmakers fail to even meet the low bar for campaign-finance reporting requirements under the current rules.

To the ire of federal regulators, Thanedar repeatedly failed to disclose the financial institution his campaign used to invest donor dollars, prompting several letters to the campaign’s treasurer: Thanedar himself. (The congressman clarified in April that his campaign used LPL Financial.)

Where lawmakers’ campaigns do their banking is often a partisan affair.

At least 86 incumbent Democrats park their campaign funds at Amalgamated Bank, a unionized and labor-aligned institution that champions accessibility and affordable housing.

Republican lawmakers and presidential hopefuls flock to Chain Bridge Bank, founded by former Republican Sen. Peter Fitzgerald.

Beyond standard banking, other members employ wealth managers to grow their campaign cash.

Janney Montgomery Scott, a Philadelphia-based wealth management firm that predates the Civil War, is particularly popular: In recent years, nearly three-dozen campaign committees have hired the firm, according to NOTUS’ review of FEC records.

The campaigns of Reps. Ritchie Torres (D-New York), Pete Aguilar (D-California) and Jim Himes (D-Connecticut) each pay five- or six figures annually to Janney Montgomery Scott in various management or brokerage fees. Each has pulled in six-figure sums this cycle alone via their investments. Torres’ total is nearly $900,000.

No incumbent Republicans bank with the firm.

The campaign of Rep. Virginia Foxx (R-North Carolina) has paid steadily increasing four-figure quarterly fees to Blue Trust, a Christian wealth management firm dedicated to bringing “financial expertise and biblical wisdom together.”
Virginia Foxx AP-24346025185857 (4000x2667, AR: 1.50)In 2024, Foxx reported $127,662 in “Realized Capital Gains on Investment” via Blue Trust. (Foxx’s campaign did not respond to a request for comment).

Republican Michael Carbonara is the founder of the fintech firm Ibanera, and his tenure as CEO overlapped with the first few months of his bid to represent Florida’s 22nd Congressional District.

In that time, his congressional campaign made sizable purchases of Bitcoin and Ethereum through Ibanera, paying thousands of dollars in fees to the company he still ran, according to federal records.

Carbonara’s campaign sold the Ethereum stake for $169,649 in November, a week after stepping down as chief executive, realizing a roughly 80% gain on his investment. Last quarter alone, he reported $1.86 million in cryptocurrency liquidations. Bitcoin’s price, meanwhile, has tumbled.

Carbonara did not respond to a request for comment.

Roots of campaign investing

The practice of political campaigns investing donor dollars has a long history.

Two decades before former Sen. Bob Menendez (D-New Jersey) went to prison over a bribery scheme that saw him receive payoffs in cash and gold bars, his campaign spent years trading stocks in various individual companies.

Eight of those companies were gold mines — literally. Among them: Glamis Gold, Harmony Gold, Newmont Mining and Goldcorp.

Former President Barack Obama’s 2008 campaign earned $1.58 million from bank interest alone. In 2024, the presidential campaign committee inherited by then-Vice President Kamala Harris after President Joe Biden dropped out pulled in $1.35 million in interest via Amalgamated Bank. Both were simple cases of campaign cash accumulating interest over time.

Trump-aligned PACs Trump 47 Committee and Never Surrender brought in over $1 million in “interest revenue” from their Chain Bridge Bank accounts in 2024 and 2025, respectively.

Other campaigns have taken riskier approaches to their investments.

Several Trump administration officials retained their campaign accounts after leaving office, and the old committees continue to net investment gains.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy departed the House in 2019 and hasn’t run for elected office since. But his old campaign has earned more than $1 million in unspecified “investment gains” across the past several years, FEC records indicate.

Duffy, ever the family man, recently contributed $1 million in campaign funds to Northwoods Future, the super PAC supporting his son-in-law, Michael Alfonso, who is running for Congress in Wisconsin.

Perhaps no other former member of Congress has pulled in as much investment income as Trump loyalist Devin Nunes.
Devin Nunes AP-21343821074979 (6774x4516, AR: 1.50)When he left Congress to oversee Trump’s media venture Truth Social, Nunes had $11 million in his congressional campaign coffers. That figure ballooned to $15.5 million during his time out of office via funds placed with Edward Jones Investments, a remarkable sum that his lawyer told federal regulators could be for “a potential future election.” Last quarter alone, he reported pulling in $1.5 million from his investment account.

Nunes’ campaign did not respond to questions about its specific investments.

Nunes is one of several former lawmakers teasing a future run to justify his campaign’s continued existence.

Tom Byrne, the son of former New Jersey Gov. Brendan Byrne, never made it into elected office despite House and Senate bids over 25 years ago. Over the years, Byrne has mulled another statewide run and has grown his campaign cash in a Charles Schwab account, bringing in over $880,220 this cycle alone.

Now, in his 70s and facing questions from federal regulators, Byrne said he’s still on the lookout for an opportunity, with his campaign telling the FEC: “it is hard to predict when another [statewide] opening may occur but it is an effort to level the playing field versus the number of self-financing statewide candidates in NJ.”

Former Rep. Cliff Stearns (R-Florida) is using a similar tactic to keep his campaign operational and collecting interest over a decade after leaving Congress. Late last year, Stearns, now 85, told federal regulators that he would wind down his committee — with a significant caveat: “We will continue to move to terminate the committee … unless we decide to be a candidate for federal office again.”

Former Democratic Rep. Joseph P. Kennedy II of Massachusetts, the elder brother of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., has maintained his personal campaign committee — “Citizens For Joe Kennedy 1988” — as a de facto investment vehicle for more than 25 years after leaving office.
JosephKennedyII (2023x1530, AR: 1.32)As Kennedy racked up “dividend income, interest income, quarterly portfolio appreciation, and capital gains,” the campaign repeatedly assured federal regulators in recent years that any expenses would be “for legal and accounting purposes in connection with keeping the committee open.”

The campaign, which did not respond to a request for comment, regularly pulls in hundreds of thousands of dollars annually in investment income.

As of July 30, Kennedy’s old committee reported having more than $1.3 million in its account — after earning more than $129,000 between April 1 and June 30 from investments with Goldman Sachs, according to FEC records.

The FEC recommends that the dormant campaign accounts of retired or deceased lawmakers be wound down within six months, but there is no hard rule requiring that deadline to be met. Dormant campaign accounts with surplus cash can, by law, donate the money to charity, transfer it to political party committees, disgorge it to the U.S. Treasury or — as is so often the case — just sit on it.

Rep. Tom Lantos (D-California) died while in office in 2008, but it took four years to fully close his committee, which continued to collect interest income across eight bank accounts. The campaign ultimately contributed the proceeds to the Lantos Foundation for Human Rights and Justice — $846,408 across three donations.

Former Rep. John LaFalce (D-New York), who left Congress in 2023, died last year. But his campaign committee lived on with money in its account — until September, when the committee emptied out the remaining $112,820 and gave it to the nonprofit Community Foundation for Greater Buffalo.

As for Foley, the late house speaker from Spokane, Washington, his campaign is managed by his widow and former chief of staff, Heather Foley, who did not respond to a request for comment.
Heather.Foley (4632x3118, AR: 1.49)Every so often, FEC officials ask her what the campaign intends to do with its cash on hand.

And just as often, she replies: “I wrote you previously that I do not intend to spend any of the campaign funds left [after] my husband’s death for personal use.”

“As soon as I have accumulated sufficient funds,” she writes, “I intend to give it to the Spokane Parks Foundation.”

entries.title: Won't You Be My Neighborhood Commissioner?
entries.content:
Good morning, D.C. In today’s newsletter: Advisory neighborhood commissioners, Montgomery County schools and a NYC-DC crossover.





THE LATEST

No one is on the ballot for a good chunk of the District’s advisory neighborhood commissioner positions ahead of tomorrow’s nomination deadline.

Of 345 ANC positions, 58 had no listed candidates as of Saturday. Though the unpaid position isn’t the flashiest in D.C. politics, ANC commissioners are vital neighborhood voices, advising the government on community issues like local zoning decisions. Some, including Mayor Muriel Bowser, go on to higher office.

“I'm not concerned about the vacancies that are on the nominating list, and I probably wouldn't be concerned until after the deadline,” Kent Boese, head of D.C.’s ANC office, told NOTUS. There are fewer vacancies this cycle than there were two years ago, Boese said, and many candidates file right before the deadline or launch write-in campaigns closer to November.

The vacancies are an opportunity for advocacy groups like the Washington Area Bicyclist Association. The nonpartisan nonprofit circulated an email this week urging members in empty districts to apply.

“We do want to encourage the District to create safe transportation infrastructure, including bike lanes, bus priority projects, and working with the ANCs is a great way to do it,” Seth Grimes, an organizer with WABA, told NOTUS. “Many times vacancies are hard to fill. There are no candidates, and so we thought, well, why not use our database and reach out to people?”

WABA has filled nine vacant ANC spots with its members since March 2025, Grimes said.





FROM THE DISTRICT

President Donald Trump is considering removing U.S. Attorney for D.C. Jeanine Pirro from her post, CNN reports. Pirro, a longtime Trump ally, recently angered the president when her office dismissed all charges against David Hearn, the Olympic canoeist who was arrested on suspicion of vandalizing the Reflecting Pool. Pirro’s office said the damage was more likely due to a botched job by the contractor, not widespread vandalism as Trump has repeatedly claimed. On Monday, Trump said Pirro “folded like an umbrella.”





FROM VIRGINIA

Amazon wants to build four data centers on George Washington University’s Ashburn campus, which the company bought this year for $427 million, the Loudoun Times-Mirror reports. Amazon got its application in ahead of a fall meeting in which Loudoun County officials will weigh a data center moratorium as they consider how to regulate the industry.





FROM MARYLAND

Montgomery County redrew its public school boundaries this spring, but the debate didn’t end there. Some parents are suing, saying the plan illegally closes one of the county’s most prestigious high schools, Jeff Barker writes for NOTUS.





FROM YOUR FEED

https://x.com/binarybits/status/2083922173828206690A tweet attempting to map New York City boroughs onto the DMV made the rounds over the weekend. Our team has some thoughts:

  • “It is genuinely hard to think of a single thing College Park, Maryland, has in common with the Upper West Side. And I say that as a proud Maryland alum.” — Michael Errigo, deputy editor
  • “Comparing Capitol Hill to New Jersey is a choice.” — Shamira Muhammad, D.C. reporter
  • "This is pretty perfect social media content: It plays on D.C.'s occasional insecurities of not being NYC, it makes sweeping generalizations about D.C.'s neighborhoods that miss loads of local nuance, and, despite my best efforts not to, I end up arguing with people about it." — Martin Austermuhle, D.C. reporter




WHAT YOU GET FOR $800,000

Kenyon St Real Estate 2 (2000x1333, AR: 1.50)
Listed for $799,900, this two-bedroom, two-bathroom home features solid oak hardwood floors, modern finishes and an open-concept living space.

Guess where this listing is sold:

  1. Maryland
  2. Virginia 
  3. D.C.
We’ll let you know tomorrow how many of you got it right.





SPORTS

The MLB trade deadline has officially passed, and the Nats turned out to be both buyers and sellers.

After adding an arm last week, Washington made three trades in the 24 hours before Monday’s 6 p.m. deadline. They sent out infielder Luis García Jr., pitcher Foster Griffin and outfielder Christian Franklin. In return they got back eight more pitchers, some of whom are expected to contribute right away.NOTUS’ Jesse Dougherty broke down the Garcia deal, calling it both strategically sound and emotionally fraught for fans.

Training camp update: NOTUS’ Martenzie Johnson reports that the Commanders’ offensive struggles may have been greatly exaggerated. On Monday in Ashburn, Jayden Daniels got the unit rolling. He completed multiple impressive touchdown passes, and the offensive line held up much better than it did last week.

What to Watch Today

MLB: Nationals at Phillies, 6:40 p.m. (MLB.TV)

entries.content:
Today’s notice: What did we learn from the Todd Blanche saga? What to watch for in Michigan tonight. Trump gives Iran another one last chance. And: A deep dive into how politicians make money investing donor money.





THE LATEST

YOLO no mo’. Did we all overhype the vision of a swashbuckling crew of wronged Republican senators out for revenge against Donald Trump? Sens. Thom Tillis (R-North Carolina) and John Cornyn (R-Texas) finally agreed to advance acting Attorney General Todd Blanche’s nomination for the permanent job on the wings of what NOTUS’ Derek Hawkins reports is an all-but-toothless promise to unwind the $1.8 billion “anti-weaponization fund” deal Trump struck with the DOJ. It was less YOLO and more YOFET (You Only Fold Every Time).

That comes after Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-Louisiana), the chair of the Senate health committee Trump eagerly bumped from reelection, voted last week to advance the president’s nominees to run the CDC and HHS’s disaster and public-health-crisis response office despite expressing strong reservations about both. Like Tillis and Cornyn, Cassidy eventually said he trusted the nominees to do the right thing, and voted for them. “You can’t have perfection,” he said.

The key difference between how these senators treated controversial nominees before Trump squashed their careers and after is tone. The president got his nominees past the senators with some light grumbling before, and stronger grumbling after. But he got them through.

“I think we did the best we could,” Cornyn told NOTUS’ Igor Bobic when asked about the deal he cut with Blanche to earn his support. But not everyone seems to agree. NOTUS’ Al Weaver reports that a couple of Republicans who have voted against controversial Trump 2.0 nominees before — Sens. Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and Susan Collins of Maine — said they were still not totally ready to sign on to the Blanche confirmation vote. But there are also signs they might not stand in the way for long, either. Murkowski called the deal Tillis and Cornyn cut a “pretty good step.”

Open tabs: The 2026 Midterms: Primary Turnout Trends as of July (Bipartisan Policy Center); A federal judge lets DHS proceed with a border wall through a small Texas town’s levee system (AP); Author of Democrats’ 2024 Autopsy Releases ‘Missing’ Chapter (NOTUS); Manufacturing survey shows inflation worries ‘worse than pandemic era,’ adding to Fed pressure (CNBC)





From Michigan


Sound smart watching the Michigan Democratic Senate primary tonight. The thing to keep an eye on, from NOTUS’ Alex Roarty: turnout. One independent analysis of tonight’s vote, shared with Alex, predicted 1.6 million people would vote in the primary. If the number trends higher, that portends well for progressive Abdul El-Sayed, who polls best with people who don’t regularly vote. If fewer people turn out, however, that’s good news for establishment candidate Haley Stevens.

B-plot to watch: The 13th Congressional District, which includes a sizable chunk of Detroit and some of its suburbs. Rep. Shri Thanedar is the incumbent Democrat, and party-aligned groups that have wanted to dislodge him for some time now think they have the person to do it in democratic socialist state lawmaker Donavan McKinney. NOTUS’ Christa Dutton explores a side of this race that doesn’t get as much attention: the personality part. Many people in Washington see Thanedar as kind of an odd guy, and have not rallied to his cause like they have other Democrats under pressure from the left. Thanedar will tell you this is a real thing, but also shrugs it off. “It’s not like a high school,” he told Christa. “I’m not trying to be the most popular member of Congress.”

From South Carolina


The new Sen. Graham out-MAGAs the last one. That was the main takeaway from last night’s South Carolina Republican Senate primary debate, where Sen. Darline Graham faced four candidates hoping to take the seat she was appointed to after her brother passed. Graham mentioned Trump had endorsed her in her opening remarks, and proceeded to make it impossible for any candidate on stage to be closer to the president than she was.

“I am all for getting rid of the filibuster — this is where I differ from my brother — because eventually the Democrats are going to get rid of it anyway,” Graham said during a conversation about the SAVE America Act.

The only candidate offering any kind of alternative was Mark Sanford, the former governor and congressman. He offered the lone MAGA-skeptical commentary on stage, dinging the president on spending and the war in Iran, but said he also supports the SAVE Act and pointed out he voted with Trump “90% of the time” when he was in Congress.

From the White House


Yet another last chance for Iran. From an Oval Office Q&A yesterday:

Reporter: Mr. President, this is at least the fifth time you’ve called off airstrikes against Iran since April to negotiate. What is your message to the American people who are wondering what has changed this time? Why should it be any different?

Trump: Well, you don’t know. I don’t know. I think we’re maybe going to get something, but I want to give them every last chance before decapitation.





NOTUS PERSPECTIVES

With Sens. John Cornyn and Thom Tillis agreeing to support Todd Blanche’s nomination for attorney general, Matt K. Lewis asks: What is wrong with Republicans?

NEW ON NOTUS

Following the money: campaign cash investments. Former House Speaker Tom Foley died in 2013 but his campaign account remains active, yielding a small profit this year from investments. Many campaigns invest funds and earn returns, which is legal and nets large fees for investment advisers. But the process is opaque, and it can be difficult to discern exactly what’s going on. NOTUS’ Mark Alfred takes a dive into the records for a detailed read on how this works, what kind of money these campaigns are making and the potential questions about conflicts of interest the practice raises.
